testcase: Go renamed model customization
query:
title: Go generated model rename

question: Our stable Go SDK has a model named A. I renamed the TypeSpec model to B and added @renamedFrom(Versions.v2, "A"), but regeneration still removes the exported Go type A. How can I keep the released Go type name?
ground_truth: Use a Go-scoped client name on the current TypeSpec model, for example @@clientName(B, "A", "go") in client.tsp, then regenerate and inspect the compatibility diff. Removing exported type A breaks existing callers. @renamedFrom describes the specification's version history; it does not by itself preserve the name in the current generated Go API.

testcase: Go renamed property customization
query:
title: Go field renamed after TypeSpec update

question: I renamed property a to b in my TypeSpec model Test and added @renamedFrom(Versions.v2, "a"). Our released Go struct has A, but regeneration replaces it with B. How do I keep A for Go without changing the other languages?
ground_truth: Apply a Go-scoped client name to the current TypeSpec property, for example @@clientName(Test.b, "a", "go") in client.tsp. Regenerate and verify the Go field remains A. Renaming an exported field breaks callers; target Test.b in the TypeSpec source rather than the generated .go field.

testcase: Go enum constant rename customization
query:
title: Go enum value rename

question: In my TypeSpec enum Test, I renamed member a to b with @renamedFrom(Versions.v2, "a"). The wire value hasn't changed, but the generated Go constant name has. Will this break callers, and how can I retain the old Go name?
ground_truth: Yes, callers referencing the released constant can break even with an unchanged wire value. Apply Go-scoped client naming to the current TypeSpec enum member, for example @@clientName(Test.b, "a", "go"), and regenerate. Inspect the resulting constant name because the Go emitter's naming transformations can differ from the source spelling.

testcase: Go property type change is breaking
query:
title: Go exported property type change

question: I used @typeChangedFrom to change a response property from string to int32. Our generated Go field now changes from *string to *int32. I thought the versioning decorator handled this, so why is the SDK change still considered breaking?
ground_truth: Changing an exported Go field from *string to *int32 requires callers to change their code. The decorator records specification evolution, not source compatibility of the current SDK. Review affected releases and the valid wire contract with Go owners to determine mitigation or an approved break. A naming override cannot repair a changed field type.

testcase: Go removed operation review
query:
title: Go operation removed from stable SDK

question: We removed an operation from our new API version using @removed. Specification validation passes, but regeneration deletes a method used by our stable Go consumers. Do I still need Go breaking-change review?
ground_truth: Yes. Deleting a public Go method is a breaking change even when specification validation passes. Identify the affected released callers and service/version contract, then work with Go reviewers on a supported mitigation or an explicitly approved break under the applicable policy. Specification validation and ARM approval do not replace Go SDK compatibility review.

testcase: Go required parameter addition
query:
title: Added required Go operation parameter

question: Our Go method used to take ctx, resourceName, and options. I added a required region parameter in the spec, and generation now puts it before options. We're adding functionality, so why does validation flag this as a breaking change?
ground_truth: Existing calls no longer match the Go method signature because the new argument is required. An additive service feature can therefore be source-breaking in the SDK. Check whether the service contract permits a compatible optional or defaulted design, or another supported mitigation. Otherwise, take the change through Go breaking-change review rather than simply suppressing the detector.

testcase: Go response type change review
query:
title: Go operation response model changes

question: We changed the response model for one of our service operations. The HTTP response is still 200, but the regenerated Go response field has a different type. Why is the SDK comparison reporting a breaking change?
ground_truth: The HTTP status does not determine Go source compatibility. A changed public response field type can break assignments and field access in existing callers. Compare the old and new generated SDK surfaces and the supported wire response with Go reviewers to choose a valid mitigation or approved break. Keeping only the method name unchanged is insufficient.

testcase: Go approved and suppression labels differ
query:
title: Go approval versus suppression

question: I see separate labels for Go SDK breaking-change approval and Go SDK suppression approval in our review workflow. Do they mean the same thing? Can I reuse either approval for later changes?
ground_truth: They represent different scoped decisions: approval of an assessed SDK change versus permission to suppress a gate. Check the current workflow, branch, and exact changes covered by the reviewer decision. One label does not automatically grant the other or cover later changes. The required labels must be applied by authorized reviewers.

testcase: Go ARM signoff is not SDK approval
query:
title: ARM review passed but Go names changed

question: ARM reviewers accepted my operation-ID rename because the HTTP URI and method stayed the same. Regeneration removes the old method from our stable Go SDK. Does the ARM approval cover this Go change too?
ground_truth: No. ARM acceptance of the service contract is separate from Go SDK compatibility approval. Removing a released Go method breaks callers even if HTTP behavior is unchanged. Preserve the old Go name through supported client customization where possible, inspect the generated diff, and obtain the appropriate Go review decision.

testcase: Go preview break needs release context
query:
title: Breaking change before first Go GA

question: Our Go SDK is still preview-only and hasn't had a stable release. Regeneration removes an empty model. Can we accept that change before our first GA, or do I still need approval?
ground_truth: Preview-only status and the empty model are relevant context, but they are not automatic approval. Confirm the release history, actual generated API impact, affected consumers, and applicable preview policy, then present the evidence to Go owners for a scoped decision. Not every preview break can be assumed acceptable.

testcase: Go closed enum versus extensible union
query:
title: Adding future SKU values

question: We're defining our new API's SKU as union Sku { Basic: "Basic", Premium: "Premium", string }. My teammate suggested a closed enum because we only have two values today. Which representation should we use if we may add more SKUs later?
ground_truth: Keep the extensible union with the string scalar if the value set can grow. A closed enum fixes the allowed values and can make future additions a compatibility problem across API versions. Azure core's no-enum guidance favors the open representation for extensible values; version enums are a separate allowed case.

testcase: Go release-branch change needs scoped evidence
query:
title: Reusing an older Go approval

question: The Go owners approved our earlier specification change on a development branch. I'm now preparing a release-branch change that also renames a public Go field. Can I use the earlier approval, or does the field rename need another review?
ground_truth: Check whether the earlier decision explicitly covers this exact field rename and release context. An approval for a development-branch change does not automatically cover a new release break. Assess the public field rename, preserve the released name through supported customization where possible, and obtain authorized approval for any remaining break.

testcase: Go stuttering-cut customization target
query:
title: Go changelog uses a shortened model name

question: My TypeSpec model is WebPubSubSettings, but it appears as Settings in the Go changelog for package webpubsub. Which name should I target in client.tsp when I customize it for Go?
ground_truth: Target the actual TypeSpec model WebPubSubSettings. The Go emitter trims a matching package prefix to avoid stuttering, so the generated name Settings is not necessarily a source symbol. Apply the Go-scoped customization to the source model and inspect the regenerated name.

testcase: Go LRO customization uses bare operation
query:
title: Go Begin method rename

question: I renamed our TypeSpec LRO operation from create to provision. The generated Go method changed from BeginCreate to BeginProvision. How should I write the client naming customization to keep BeginCreate?
ground_truth: Customize the current TypeSpec operation provision to the old bare operation name create for Go, for example @@clientName(provision, "create", "go"), qualified with your namespace as needed. The Go emitter adds Begin for the LRO, so do not target BeginProvision or include the generated prefix in the override. Regenerate and confirm BeginCreate remains.

testcase: Go pager customization uses bare operation
query:
title: Go pager method rename

question: I renamed our paged TypeSpec operation listByResourceGroup to enumerateByResourceGroup, and regeneration replaced NewListByResourceGroupPager in Go. How can I preserve the released pager method name?
ground_truth: Apply Go-scoped client naming to the current TypeSpec operation enumerateByResourceGroup with the old name listByResourceGroup. The Go emitter supplies New and Pager, so use the bare operation name rather than the generated New...Pager method. Regenerate and check that NewListByResourceGroupPager is retained in the public API.

testcase: Go client customization entry point
query:
title: Set up Go client.tsp customization

question: I need Go-specific naming overrides without changing our service spec for the other clients. Where should I put client.tsp, and should main.tsp import it? I've only edited generated .go files so far.
ground_truth: Put client.tsp alongside main.tsp. client.tsp imports main.tsp and the client-generator-core library, not the other way around. Add supported Go-scoped naming overrides there and use the client-generation entry-point workflow to regenerate. Editing generated .go files alone is not a durable customization.

testcase: Go reviewer comment before final approval
query:
title: SDK reviewer requested regeneration

question: My required Go checks are green. A reviewer asked me to regenerate after fixing a name in client.tsp, but I haven't regenerated yet. Can I request final approval, or do I need to rerun generation first?
ground_truth: Regenerate first so the reviewed naming fix is present in the SDK output. Confirm the resulting public names and rerun the affected checks, then ask the reviewer to confirm the change. Green checks on the previous output do not validate the new source customization.

testcase: Go merge blocked by requested changes
query:
title: Go SDK requested changes

question: My Go SDK change has no conflicts and all required CI checks pass, but a reviewer is still requesting changes because we removed a stable field. What do I need to resolve before merging?
ground_truth: Resolve the removed stable field's compatibility impact and the blocking review. Restore the field through a supported mitigation or obtain an authorized decision on the break, update generated artifacts as needed, and ask the reviewer to confirm the resolution. Passing CI does not remove the requested-changes blocker.

testcase: Go prepare pipeline for new module
query:
title: New Go module release preparation

question: We've generated a new ARM Go module, and it compiles successfully. My reviewer says we still need release pipeline preparation. What else should I check before asking for approval?
ground_truth: Compilation and release pipeline preparation are separate steps. Follow the reviewer's instruction and the current new-module ARM release guidance to confirm the required pipeline exists and preparation has completed. Also satisfy the remaining review and check requirements before requesting approval. A successful compile does not prove pipeline preparation has run.

testcase: Go reviewers must come from actual owners
query:
title: Who should approve my Go SDK change?

question: My Go SDK change has passed the required checks, and all blocking comments are resolved. The requested reviewer is a team rather than an individual. Who should I follow up with for final approval?
ground_truth: Follow up with the requested team or the verified matching CODEOWNERS for the package. Final approval needs an authorized reviewer. An individual owner cannot be identified from the team-only context here; use the actual ownership and review information rather than guessing a person's handle.

testcase: Go detailed generation artifacts
query:
title: Go SDK automation only reports generic failure

question: My SDK validation run reports "Errors occurred while generating SDK" and "Failed to read generateOutput.json". I haven't found the inner generation log yet. Where can I get more details to understand what's failing?
ground_truth: Use the SDK-Validation guidance to download the detailed generation logs and artifacts, then find the first concrete error. Missing generateOutput.json may be a consequence of an earlier generation or environment failure, not the root cause. Share that diagnostic and the relevant generation configuration before choosing a TypeSpec fix.

testcase: Go private repo still fails after public incident fix
query:
title: Private Go validation still fails

question: The owners say they fixed a shared checkout-tooling failure in public automation, but our private spec repository still reports the same checkout error. Do we need to update anything in the private environment?
ground_truth: Check the tooling version or commit and synchronization state used by the private run. A public automation fix does not prove the private environment has received it. Send the current private run logs to the engineering-system owners, confirm whether a sync or tooling update is needed, and rerun after it is applied. This checkout failure is not evidence that your service model needs a change.

testcase: Go test proxy NuGet failure is not proven ESRP failure
query:
title: Go CI test-proxy install cannot reach NuGet

question: Our Go CI fails when installing the .NET-based test proxy because it can't reach NuGet. I suspect this might be an ESRP incompatibility, but the log doesn't show an ESRP error. How should I investigate?
ground_truth: The evidence currently points to a test-proxy installation or connectivity failure, not a confirmed ESRP issue. Inspect the install log, failing NuGet endpoint, network or proxy settings, TLS errors, and package-feed configuration. This is separate from SDK API compatibility. Keep ESRP as an unverified hypothesis unless the detailed logs support it.

testcase: Go APIView package name pending
query:
title: Go first-release package-name approval

question: Our Go release check says the package name isn't approved. The APIView discussion also has blocking comments asking us to clean up the name. What should we finish before requesting release approval?
ground_truth: Address the blocking naming comments and obtain authorized package-name or first-release approval through the API review process. That approval is distinct from approval of an API revision and from the release pipeline's approval gate. Confirm each applicable gate separately before requesting release approval.

testcase: Go merged SDK still needs release approval
query:
title: Go release pipeline waiting for approval

question: Our SDK change has merged, but the internal release pipeline is waiting for an authorized approver. I thought the merge approval was enough. Who needs to approve the release now?
ground_truth: PR approval and release pipeline approval are separate steps. Contact an authorized release approver for the matching pipeline run and have them satisfy the release gate. The merge does not bypass that gate or establish publication. Use the actual pipeline approval configuration to identify the approver rather than guessing an individual.

testcase: Go release verification exact version
query:
title: Go registry has older version

question: I'm trying to confirm that our Go module v1.1.0 was released. The build stage succeeded, but I only see v1.0.0 in the module registry. How can I verify the new version is available?
ground_truth: Check the release run's publish stage for the exact module and v1.1.0, then resolve module@v1.1.0 with go get or inspect the corresponding published version evidence. A successful build and the presence of v1.0.0 do not prove publication of v1.1.0. Treat the new release as unconfirmed until that exact version is available.

testcase: Go dependency allowlist is repository specific
query:
title: External dependency allowed by generic guidelines?

question: We want to add a third-party dependency to our Go module. It isn't listed in the repository allowlist, and we don't have an approved exception yet. The generic SDK guidelines discuss dependency tradeoffs; is that enough, or do we need Go repository approval?
ground_truth: Consult the current Go repository go.mod standards and any applicable package-specific exceptions. General dependency tradeoff guidance does not authorize a new exception to the repository policy. Obtain owner review and approval of the proposed dependency and policy change before relying on it. This does not imply that every third-party module is forbidden.

testcase: Go feature branch large diff does not waive failures
query:
title: Go feature-branch sync with failing checks

question: We merged main into our large Go SDK feature branch, and some required checks now fail. I suspect the large diff is causing it. Can we get an override, or should we investigate something first?
ground_truth: Inspect the specific required checks and their diagnostics first. Determine whether the failures are merge regressions or an unrelated infrastructure issue; diff size alone does not justify an override. Fix the actual blockers or present evidence for a scoped exception to the authorized owners. An override cannot be granted based only on the size of the change.

testcase: Go deprecation notice files
query:
title: Go SDK final deprecation patch

question: We're preparing the final patch for our retiring Go module. I've added a README notice, but I haven't changed go.mod or the changelog. Is there anything else I need for the deprecation release?
ground_truth: Add the module deprecation comment beginning // Deprecated: in go.mod and a notice in the final release's changelog, alongside the README guidance. Include accurate retirement or migration instructions, then complete the final patch's review and release process. A README edit alone is not the full documented deprecation change or proof that a deprecation release is published.

testcase: Go deprecation is not retraction
query:
title: Retiring a Go SDK module

question: Our service is retiring, and a teammate suggested retracting every Go module version to announce it. Should we do that, or use module deprecation? What's the difference?
ground_truth: Use the documented module deprecation lifecycle for normal retirement, typically a final release with the deprecation comment and retirement or migration notices. Retraction identifies problematic versions; it is not a synonym for retiring a module. Do not retract every version solely to announce normal service retirement.

testcase: Go preview GA sequence needs per-release assessment
query:
title: Go preview feature absent from first GA

question: We're planning a preview API with a feature, a first GA API without it, and a later GA API that adds it back. Our SDK work goes into main. How should we sequence the Go releases, and what compatibility checks do we need between them?
ground_truth: Plan generation, review, and release in the intended sequence, distinguishing service API versions from preview and stable Go module versions. Compare the generated Go surfaces at each step, especially removed or reintroduced symbols and compatibility for stable consumers. Sequential releases are a process option, not automatic compatibility approval, and merging into main does not prove publication.

testcase: Go major version does not establish compiler support
query:
title: Generic Go API requires newer compiler

question: We're planning a new major version of our Go SDK with a language feature that needs a newer compiler. We haven't checked whether that feature has shipped or which older Go versions our customers use. Does the major-version bump let us raise the minimum Go version?
ground_truth: A major-version bump does not establish compiler support or automatically authorize dropping older toolchains. Verify the exact feature and released compiler requirement in authoritative Go documentation, then review supported consumers, module migration, and the minimum-version policy with SDK owners. An unavailable language feature will not compile merely because the module has a new major version.
